title: Fostering Intimacy in Marriage
author: Tim Challies
summary: Tim Challies reflects on preparing a weekend marriage seminar and being convicted about a kind of intimacy many couples overlook. Physical intimacy, he argues, is real but also symbolic of a deeper unity, and many husbands and wives find it easier to bare their bodies than their souls. He admits that he and his wife Aileen are both reserved and wounded people who hold back parts of themselves, and he observes a deep longing in everyone to be known and still loved. To foster soul intimacy he proposes four practices: creating times for lengthy, uninterrupted conversation and asking good questions, assuring each other of acceptance modelled on Christ, being active in both learning and revealing since love depends on knowledge, and understanding sex as a symbol of intimacy and not the sum of it. The covenant of marriage, he says, makes deep knowledge provoke greater love and patience.
points: Physical intimacy is real but symbolic of deeper unity, and treating it as the whole of intimacy leaves emotional distance intact.
The author names the obstacles honestly as reserve, past wounds and pride about what a spouse might think.
Creating protected time for long conversation, with good questions and attentive listening, is presented as lifelong work.
Love and knowledge grow together, so the more spouses know each other the more they can love, and the more they are known the more they can be loved.
Sexual union should be consistent with a marriage lived bared in heart and soul, not an outlier of closeness.
quotes: Physical intimacy is both significant and essential to marriage, but it is not meant to be the sum total of the intimacy shared between a husband and wife.
Yet as Aileen and I have interacted with other couples, we have observed that many husbands and wives find it easier to bare their bodies than their souls.

There is an irony to this, because I am convinced there is a deep longing within each of us to be known. We want someone else to know us as we truly are and to still love us and give us their approval.

In a non-marriage relationship, deep knowledge might provoke us to recoil or walk away, but because we are bound together in the covenant of marriage, deep knowledge can only provoke greater love and greater patience with one another in our weaknesses and sins.
The degree to which we can love another person varies with the degree to which we know them, so that the more we know them, the more we can love them.

Rather than allowing the sexual union to be an outlier—a kind of intimacy that’s much deeper than any other part of our relationship—we ought to ensure it is a part of our marriage that’s consistent with living our lives bared before one another, not just in body, but in heart and soul as well.
